blocks.x: Kid Horry April 20th 1957 Rule 1
This is an interview with Kid Horry in his beautiful house in San Anselmo, California.
Sleepy Hall.
That was the voice of Mrs. Horry you just heard. Alright? Yeah. You're in business? Huh?
Yeah, I just want to watch as you talk a little while and just watch because it's not supposed to go anywhere.
When were you born?
As long 1886, December 25th. December, on Christmas Day? That's right. Is that so? And where? Laplace, Louisiana.
Now how far is that from, New Orleans?
That's 29 miles and three-tenths of a mile. Well...
That's pretty accurate.
He's taking your right to the plantation door.
That's the most precise answer I've ever had in my life. You scared me. Very good, I'll say. Thank you. Let's start over again. I'll take it. I'll do it.
You must have measured it many times.
I walked it many times, you know.

What I'd like to know from you first is how you first became interested in music. How old you were and what you were playing and so on. Well, I was about seven years old. About seven years old. And you were still in Laplace?
Yeah.
Now what instrument did you play?
Well, I first made a banjo. Yeah. And I made a ghetto.
You mean you built them yourself?
Yeah. And I made a bass.
A ghetto, dear?
A ghetto. She must put the all in.
You know what you're talking about.

What kind of banjo did you make? I made a five-string banjo. Out of what? Out of ten buckets. Mm-mm. About the banjo. Yeah, the banjo was a cut bucket, half of it down in regular buckets, you know, about this size. And cut it down about there. Yeah. Well, that was the first one. That was the first one, yeah.
And you used the metal strings on that one.
No, I was using thread and fishing cards and...
Afterwards you switched to metal.
Oh, yeah. Because they broke all the time. Yeah. When I made one loose. Out of a cigar box later on. No, a cigar box was the guitar. Oh, excuse me.
Were there any musicians in your family? No.
No.
How come you became so interested in music?
Well, I used to hear a brass band play all the time. Pickwick brass band and Arnold brass band.
Those were bands from New Orleans, you mean?
No, from one from Laplace.
Oh.
And one from Reserve. From Reserve. Just about three miles.
Who did you play with when you made these instruments?
Well, I had my own little outfit. I had the two Matthews boys and myself. We started. Yeah. Then I had another kid named White. Yeah.
And Eddie Robinson, which we called Rabbit. What instruments did they play? This was a kid band, in other words. Kid band. Like playing in the streets.
Homemade instrument, yeah. We started.
Did you call that band anything? Did you have a name for that band, which had instruments like that?
No. Yeah, we did. What did you call it? I did. We called it the Woodland Band.
The Woodland Band.
The Plantation Band.
Uh-huh. What kind of instruments did you all have?

Well, I told you, we had a homemade banjo, homemade guitar, homemade bass. How was the bass made? How was the bass made? With a big soapbox, you know, a wooden box. And worked on the handle of a neck, just like you would a regular bass, you know. And, uh... How many strings? I had four strings.
Oh, yeah?

Different sides of fishing cords, you know. Uh-huh. G-strips. Fishing cords. Yeah. Nice. You know, I used to fish and... Uh-huh. Do you have a bridge on it? Oh, yeah, a bridge. Used lots of rosin because, you know, the string.
What was the guitar made on it?
Huh?
What was it?
Great big cigar box. We used to make a big cigar box, you see. And used different sides of thread, you know.
So you had a banjo, a guitar, a bass. What else did you have? Violin. Violin. Violin.
Homemade violin, too? Homemade violin with a smaller cigar box.
Is that so? Uh-huh.
How'd they sound? Oh, it sounded good, you know. We tried to sing along with it, you know. You sang with it, huh? Uh-huh.
That's how he started out, originally. Before he had the instruments, they hummed. They had a little humming band. Oh, yeah?
Before you made the instruments?
Uh-huh. Before you made the instruments, you had a humming band? Uh-huh.
Yeah. We used to stand on the bridge, you know, at night. Over a creek. In the dark and just couldn't see anyone. No one could see us, could hear us, you know, singing on the bridge.
Hmm.
Get us a few ginger cakes and it was all right, some water.
Something for the tummies and the music for the soul. Oh, God.
You'd get three big, we called them stage planks. It was about that long and that wide, you know, three for a dime.
Did you have any rhythm instruments with this group?
Oh, afterwards, when I made the homemade instruments.
That's what I mean. What did you have? What kind of rhythm instruments?

Well, the same instrument I had. We had the guitar and the violin and bass. Banjo. And banjo. And the drum. Well, later we had the drums, you see. That came later. Yeah. Taking a big tub and then a foot pedal, you know.
Oh, yeah?
Uh-huh.
We had a regular drum set, in other words.

Yeah. It wasn't exactly what we are, you know, what we used today, you know. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. So. What kind of a tub? Uh, wash tub. Tin tub? Tin tub, yeah. And, uh, deaden it inside with cloth, you know, a rag. Yeah. Keep it from ringing too much. And it's like, boof, boof, you know.
That sounded pretty good. Yeah. Huh? Yeah. Now, where'd you play with this? Once you had this little kid band organized, where did you play?
Well, uh, I couldn't get a job, so I started promoting fish fries.
Yeah?
And I started selling beer, you know.
Where'd you get the fish from?
Huh?
Where'd you catch a fish?
Out of the Mississippi River and creeks. Was, was that place on the Mississippi River or near? Yeah, I would just, just, uh, say about, uh, about 75 feet to my.
Oh, really? That close, huh? Uh-huh.
Across the land, there you ran under there.
And his plantation that he lived on, that ran up right up to the land.
I used to keep my line in the river all the time.
Oh.
By the time I wanted a fish, I'd pull it out and throw it back in.
So tell us about these fish fries. What were they like?
Well, that, uh, catfish and different kind of fish, poachers, and potato salad. Did you make all this yourself? Why, sure.
Well, how old were you? About ten years old at the stand?
No, I wasn't quite ten. I was between seven and, I started when I was seven. When I was ten, I was going to stand playing professional with real nature of it.
Oh, yeah? Well, let's, let's.
All right.
Let's stay on this.
Let's stay under ten a while. Yeah, right.
Where did you, so, you had this, these little fish fries. Did you charge?
On the plantation, what?
How much did you charge for these things?
Well, five cents a drink, five cents for a fish sandwich. If they wanted to double, well, it's ten cents. Uh-huh.
And while they were having, you know, this is like a picnic, like a lawn party, in other words, like a little.
Well, it mostly, it was in, in, in the room, you know. Oh, this was indoors. Yeah, because the entrance would wouldn't carry out.
Oh, this was indoors.
Indoors. I see. At the time we'd find an empty house, we didn't have to rent it, just go on and bring some candle in, light it up, and go to work.
In the evening, this was at night?
At night.
Yeah, evening.
What kind of people came? Kids or grown people? Everyone more to come. Babies and everything. Uh-huh. Sell bananas and everything. Fruit.
Did many older people come?
Oh, yeah. Well, in those days, the younger people couldn't go out without the parents, you know. I see.
So the parents would bring the kids down?
Yeah. That's right.
That's right. What tunes did you play with that band? Hmm? What tunes did you play then?
We used to play Make Me a Pallet on the Floor, Think Heard, Butter, Bold, and Save, and quite a few more that I can't recall, you know, old numbers. Uh-huh.
Did you play waltzes and things like that?
Oh, yeah, waltzes and shouters. You did, huh? Mm-hmm.
Well, what did you play in the band? Which instrument?
I played all of them, but my regular instrument was the first was the banjo. Then my bass player wasn't doing so good, so I gave the guitar to Matthew. He played guitar and I played bass. Lewis.
Is that, this is not the same Matthews? Bill Matthews?
No, no, no. Lewis and Joe Matthews. Uh-huh.
Are they related?
They're brothers. Brothers, yeah. Brothers. They started out with... Not to Bill Matthews.
Not to Bill Matthews.
No.
That's just the same name.
Same name, yeah.
No relative. Well, were you able to make some money from these little operations?
Yes, I did. I was the leader, the promoter, bookkeeper, and the treasure. And the fish fryer. The fish fryer.
But he didn't stay a fish fryer long. He got girls to take over that work.
Oh, well, I was able to pay... Good little health, huh?
Mm-hmm.
Free health. I was able to pay him 50 cents a night. Well, then I was a big shot, didn't you? Sure. Yeah.
Well, were you able to save some money and so on? Would you...

Well, I saved the money until I got enough money, then I promoted a big picnic at a baseball game. An Orlean team came to play the country boys, and one of the... The park, my dad, is his first cousin, and I told him what I wanted to do, you know? Yeah. And I went to buy a real instrument, and so...
What did you buy? What instrument?

Real. That's what we're using today. I know. With what? With seven. Seven instrument. Oh, you wanted to buy instruments for everybody, you mean? Yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh. I had taken the money. I accumulated on the fish fryer, and I saved it. I kept adding to it every week. We'd play and have our fish fryer. Uh-huh. When I had enough money, I ate for the park and have a picnic after the ball game. While the game was going on, while the game was going on, while I still was selling beer and stuff, you know, and food. So they gave me everything free. When I found out what I wanted to do, my dad was coming and his partner on the plantation and the grocery store. They gave me everything I wanted. Beer and all the food and all the meat. They opened everything for me.
But you might tell what brought that on. He didn't believe in your music at first.

Yeah, I know. My dad, his first cousin, wanted me to work on the plantation after my dad had died. So I didn't like plantation work. It was a great lost tower farm. You know, my dad had died. Was sick at the time. And so he said he didn't thought I was any good.
Because he wanted to play music instead of learning how to run a plantation.
He wanted to get my job as a boss or overseer, you know.

Yes. He and his son were the only two males in the family on the Ory's plantation. Oh, I see. And it was the idea that he and the first cousin's son would eventually run the plantation as the father got old enough to not be able to do everything himself. So his female cousins, to get their father on his side, gave a party and hired his band. And when Daddy saw how all the guests loved his music from there on in, he was on Ed's side and realized he wasn't trying to get out of work after all. But he had something that should be used.
What kind of instruments did you buy when you bought real instruments? What did you buy? I showed them. I finished down there the night of the dance of the big party.
Yeah.

He came up to me. He said, you know, I'm sorry. He told me in French that he accused me of being a lazy boy. He said, you know, everyone is good for something in this world. That's right. Yeah. He said, anything I can help you, let me know.
He talked to you in French. Yeah. At this time, French was your main language. That's right.
Parisian times, too. He couldn't speak English at all.
He couldn't speak English at all. My dad didn't either. He couldn't. So you made enough on the picnic to buy the instruments. Yeah.
What kind of instruments did you buy?
Well, I bought a valve trombone, violin, twelve-string guitar. Twelve-string guitar? Yeah. With six double strings? Yeah.
Yeah.
Bass, trumpet, and drum. Mm-hmm. Seven-inch. Who played them? Well, we had two Matthews boys and Lawrence Dewey. Lawrence Dewey? Yeah.
Is he from Laplace?
Yeah.
Yes.
Two Matthews boys, one of them today, another boy named White. Name was Buller White. And Alfred Lewis played bass. Yes. And Eddie Robertson drumming myself. 된된된 된 된
What did you play first? In the band? Yeah. Val Trombone.
How did you play it? How did you know how to play it?
Well, I just picked it up on Wednesday. On a Saturday night I was playing for a dance.
Had you ever played one before?
No. I just saw the guy. Well, how did you make your notes? Well, sometimes when the brass band would be playing there for a big banquet day, you know what they call them, the ball caves, you know.
Yes.

The guy was putting the horns on and be drinking beer. I'd slip from getting one of the horns and try to blow it, you know. I didn't notice how they were putting it to the mouth, and I just kept until I got a tone.
So you were really self-taught? Yeah. Nobody taught Schrodinger how to do it?
No.
How to get a scale or anything?
No.
All by yourself? That's right. By ear?
That's right. And with an hour I could play in all the keys, you see.
Really?
I first thought I could play in one key, but I kept adding.
Did you all have to decide on which key you were going to play in?
Oh, yeah, definitely. If I'd pick up the lead, I said, follow me in B flat, E flatter. I said, all down, stay down. You can't come, stop.
Were the other boys self-taught too?
Oh, yeah.
Every one of them, yeah. They just picked up and in a few days they started to play with them. That's right. That's amazing.
Yeah. Honestly, everybody.

So once you had... Not so amazing if you think of the number of children on that plantation, and how he picked them over carefully to find the ones that were even slightly interested in the first place to start a humming group.
Did you follow the brass bands around when you were younger, when you were kids? Oh, yeah. Second line and so on, huh?

I remember sometimes they have rehearsal in a big house, you know. They wouldn't let the kids in. Sometimes they would have it at my friend's house, you know. I'd get the L and get underneath the bed, you see. And then they would play, yeah. Really?
Yeah.
You were really fascinated by music as a child, huh?

I couldn't say anything but music. Is that so? The girls were in me, but I didn't... I liked the girls all right, but I wanted music first. Music first, huh? I said, if I learn music, I can get a girl, you know. Yeah.
Oh, me oh my. What did you do? What kind of tunes did you do when you had that humming group? Same tunes?
What?
No, we... How did that work? I mean, did you really hum? Is that what you did?
We hummed, and when we know the tune itself, the melody, you know, one of us would take the melody, three-part, four-part harmony, you know.
You do three, four-part harmonies.
Yeah.
Like a barbershop quartet, kind of.
Yeah, and sometimes we couldn't get the correct chord, you know, four-part harmony. Couldn't get all the way through. We'd double up, you see. That was very good for your ear training, huh?
Yeah.

Very good. And we'd, the kids, we used to bet, if we'd hear a brass band playing, see, about a block from her, and we'd bet to see what key, to prove, you know, see which one, know what key the band was playing in. Oh, yeah? Boy, I went out every time.
Is that so? Yeah.

Like a contest to test your ears, yeah? Yeah, yeah. He still has it today, thank God. Yeah, I can hear a band playing. If I didn't hear them, I can tell what key they play. Oh, yeah? You know, on the television, the radio.
Why'd you go out on this little bridge to home?

Well, we didn't have no other place. You mean this was a little place in town? On the plantation, on the plantation. Oh, I see. Yeah. You mean it was just a good place to get together. Yeah, you see, we had lost our place, you know, and my dad and mother took me home. And it had too much mortgage on it, and I couldn't get enough money to pay it off, so I sold it and gave the money to my sisters.
Uh-huh.
And my brother, he had left home. He was in business himself. He had a grocery boy, you know, across the river. So we decided to give the girls the money, and we went for ourselves.
But when you had that homemade band, you know, you said you'd play in a little house, you'd find an empty house or something.
Yeah, I'd promote the...
Would they be just deserted houses? I mean, people left?

Well, just people move out, you know, change from one plantation to another, you know. Uh-huh. There's always an empty house, you know. And sometimes we get in the finish. People didn't have much furniture, you know. They let us come in the house and have the party.
How would you promote it?
We'd give them all the food and the beer they wanted, you know.
How would you promote or advertise it? Huh? How would you promote a thing like that in advance?
Oh, from mouth to mouth.
Mouth to mouth. Yeah.

Well, there were people around there, they'd all look for a place to go on Saturday night, you see. No place to go. They'd all flop there and get beer. What kind of plantation was this? Oh, the big sugarcane plantation. Sugarcane plantation. Yeah, big sugar mill and everything.
Oh, yeah?
And all the people from the little villages, other plantation would come.
When would you do it usually on? Saturday night or what?
Saturday night. Saturday night. Saturday night. Saturday and Sunday afternoon.
I see. Saturday night and Sunday afternoon.
They would let me run on Sunday night. They said people had to go to work early, Monday.
Monday, yeah.

I start early on Sunday afternoon, you see. Uh-huh. And when I gave them a big picnic at the park, I really charged 15 cents to come in. Uh-huh. After the game, everyone went out and came out and bought their tickets.
Oh, you first had to get out? Get out.
That paid admission to see the game. Yeah. After coming by me then, you see.
I see. Right in the baseball park, huh?
Yeah. Yeah.
In the, before that, when you had the homemade van, you could get beer and so on for the picnic?
Yeah.
So whiskey too, everything.

Oh yeah? Yeah. Even as a kid. Who, who'd you buy it from? Oh, I used to give it to my, my dad, his partner. I see. Oh. To give it to you then? Yeah. To make a profit off it. Well, they're the only one that had a liquor license on there, you see. Yeah.
Oh, so they made a profit and you made a little profit. No, they gave it to me. Oh.
He was helping me.

He was helping him out because he was his uncle. Mm-hmm. Did you have to do a lot of experimenting with these homemade instruments to get them to sound right? Or, or did, did you just know how to make them?
Well, after I made the banjo, well, I had a good idea, you know, how the others would sign up and I just kept working on them.
Did you have to, like on the violin, did you have to make any of those openings in the box or anything? Yeah, I got a hole, yeah.
Yeah?
Oh, that scroll stuff?
Did you make little holes?

Yeah. I didn't have any saw to saw them, you know. I take a red iron, small iron, you know, and just keep it burning and make it crooked. I see. You know, just like with the bass violin or violin. Yes. In the hole, I guess, oh yeah.
Yeah, like F holes.
Yeah, burned it out, you know, very thin wood, eight of them, I think, you know. Uh-huh. You know, a cigar box.
Yes, yes, sure.

So it's not too, but did they get a pretty, did they get a pretty good sound? They just found, yeah, in a room like this. Yeah? Yeah. And you all sang and played? Sang, yeah. Only thing we used, lots of rosin, you know. We had the boy on the thing, I guess, you know. On the bass, you mean? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. We had the grip on it, thread, and the cards, and we'd break lots of strings, dude.
Had you been to New Orleans at this time? Had you ever gone to the city? Or what?
Uh... Do you remember the first time?
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. No. Later you went. No, I had never... You'd never been to New Orleans? No.
Did bands come from New Orleans sometimes to La Placar Reserve? Yeah. Yeah. So you heard bands once in a while, in other words?
Yeah. And bands come out there every payday in the wintertime, you know, doing the sugar grinding.
Oh, every payday there was a band, huh?
Yeah.
Do you remember some of the bands that came?
Yeah.
Who came?
Peyton, Dave... I think their name was Dave Peyton. Dave Peyton, yeah. Yeah, and Galloway.
Yeah.
They was in Bolden, King Bolden time, you know.
Mm-hmm. Did Bolden ever come?

No, Bolden passed through there. He used to pass through there going to Baton Rouge playing on excursion. Oh, I see. I mean, I see the advertisement, you know, hearing from other people talking that... Was he pretty well known in... Who?
Bolden. Was he well known even in places like La Placar?

Oh, yeah. His name meant something. Sure, sure. He used to put all those excursions, you know, from Baton Rouge, all in the Baton Rouge. Mm-hmm. And he stopped at the class and played tune, you know, in the baggage car. Uh-huh. And we used to go to Station Island and listen to that.
What was that on a railway station?
Railway station. Yazool, Mississippi Valley.
What?
Yazool and Mississippi Valley Railroad. From Baton Rouge.
From New Orleans to Baton Rouge. That's right. And it stopped in La Placar?
Yeah.
And you mean the band played when the train stopped?

Yeah, when the train stopped, yeah. Where would they play from? From the baggage car. From the baggage car? They stand right in the door with a horn, didn't it? And what do you... And the bass drummed behind them, right? And would the people... Orchard gathered, right?
Yeah? Did you always go?
Huh?
Were you always there?
Yeah, I didn't miss a tree. Uh-huh. See, the train stops on the way.
Just to play? Just to play. I mean, they played on the stops.
Lots of people who board the train, you know, the elder people.
Oh, I see. And go on. Yeah.
It was like an excursion train, huh? Yeah, excursion train.
From New Orleans to Baton Rouge. So this would be a way of advertising.

Then they'd have a dance in Baton Rouge. Yeah. They'd have a dance in Baton Rouge. They'd dance all afternoon and it leaves probably... Well, the day from the time they get there, let's see, they should arrive Baton Rouge here about 9 o'clock, 9.15. And then about 11 o'clock the days would start. Then the dance took until about 4.30, then the train leaves about 5, and all the little afternoon, about 8 o'clock that night would come back through the plot on the way to Baton Rouge. Now let's talk about... But it wouldn't play, come back, you know. Just going. You weren't going. Trying to get people to go. Well, it was advertising, you know. Yeah.
Now once you got your band organized with regular instruments, what happened next? What did you do?
Well, I played up and down the road from Laplace to Baton Rouge, all the sawmill towns, and for Kenner.
How old are you by this time?

Well, I was on the stand playing when I was 10 years old. I played my first job when I was 10 years old. Ten. Played for a big... Playing regular Val trombone. Val trombone. All the real instruments. Mm-hmm.
Was the good Val was a good instrument?
Mm-hmm.
A well-made, a good instrument?
No. It wasn't real good. Had a few holes in it, and I plastered up with soap, you know.
Oh, yeah?
The first one. Uh-huh. Only paid $4, so I... Uh-huh. But I mean, the real ones, I had a good one. Yeah. Had a yoke. Yeah. After I gave the picnic, you see. I see. And I bought real ones.
How old were the other kids?
We all were arranged, but in the same age.
All about the same.
Mm-hmm.
What did you wear? How did you all dress then?

Well, we dressed the way best we could, you know. Until I got the picnic and got real instrument, then I bought all coats, you know, to match, you know. You did? Any kind of dress, yeah. What kind of coats were they? Any kind of sport coats, you know. Uh-huh. Pedalers used to come around the house. You can buy them for 25 cents a week, you know. Oh, right.
So, you mean, you bought the uniforms for the whole band that way, huh?
Yeah. Some of the boys that wear them out, I'd take them home after their job. I'd take them to my house. They're going to be clean for the next job, you know. Yeah.
What did they look like? Were they just regular jackets or...

Regular. What color were they? Well, they're gray and blue, you know. As long as they're all the same color, yeah. Uh-huh. Nothing expensive. Uh-huh. But it's clothes that you'd pay more money today for. Did you wear a necktie? Oh, yeah. Short and necktie? White shirt? White shirt, yeah. And we wore... Bow tie or what? Yeah. Bow tie, mostly. Little bow tie? Very stylish. Yeah.
But they were just like regular jackets, is that right? Or were they different from that?

What? Coats? Mm-hmm. No, regular street clothes like we wear. They're like we wear now, you know. But we mostly had... Summertime had... I call it the pongee, you know. Light... Very lightweight, so warm. Yes. It was very cheap, too, you see. Uh-huh. We in those days would get a suit of clothes, a $7.95, a good suit of clothes, you know. Yes. Oh, we didn't have any clothes at all when we started, you know. Oh, man, that's enough to get by, look clean. Yes. But finally, we made it.
Did you hear any other music besides what the brass bands were playing around when you were a kid?
Yeah, as I told, uh, that's where, uh, Peyton, uh, Dave Peyton band and the Galloway band used to come out over past every pay they do in the winter. From you on. I see. From New Orleans. That one.
Those were regular dance bands, huh? Yeah, an accordion band. Oh, yeah? And guitar, most of the string music, yeah. Most of the string music? And Galloway, he had horns.
He had horns? Yeah. More like a jazz band. Yeah. One was a string band. And they'd play on paydays? Yeah. Did they play out in the fields or in a closed place?
In the big houses.
Big houses or barns? Yeah, big barns. And did people dance? Oh, yeah.
Dancing? Dancing.
What kind of tunes did they play?
They played almost all Buddy Bolden tunes.

Where did Buddy Bolden get his tunes? Where did Buddy Bolden get his tunes? Did he make them up himself? Or how did they happen? He got more of them from the Holy Roller Church. From the church? From the Holy Roller Church. And he would change them a little. Oh, yeah.

Yeah, well, I'll show you that he put his own feeling to it, you know. Uh-huh. Such tunes as what do you think he got from there? Oh, like the Saints and all this stuff like that. Well, look who's here. Hello.
This is Babette.
Made me a pilot on the front. I was bold and on, you know. It was. He wrote it. Yeah.
Baby, you look beautiful. Woo!
That's my little daughter. Very cute. Hi, Babette.
Hi, Babette.

You should have seen her one way around. He's in Paris. Isn't she pretty? They all started, after they yelled for him, we were still on the train, they started yelling for Babette. So he stood her up at the window of our compartment, and with all the flash bulbs going off, the band playing, and people yelling, her all for Babette, she was blowing kisses to them and smiling.
I love that.
Just like a little old professional.
How old is she now?
She'll be three in June. Three in June?
Mm-hmm. She had a rhythm to it. You want to see her dance? Yeah. Come on today.
Kid Ory, April 20th, 1957, Reel 2. So you think that Bolden got most of his tunes from church, huh?
Yeah.
You mean... Oh, we're all. Is that so? Ooh! What dampness. You said that Bolden got his music from the church, and then you're going to say something else. You said, but also...

Well, he had quite a few of his own compositions, you know? Yeah? Which makes me a pallet on the floor. And some for the rag men, you said. Then... Thought I heard Buddy Bolden say it, but he's not my tune. And he got lots of his tunes from the rag men. He used to blow a toy horn. Yeah. And the guy used to play tune, and Bolden used to get ideas of a tune from that.
I don't... Did you... The rag men? You mean...

Yeah, rag men. Come around to buy old rag tunes? Yeah. He used to play tunes, you mean? Yeah, on a... It's like a kid used for a Christmas toy horn, you know? A kazoo. Kazooie. Uh-huh. And, you know, long, about that long. You mean this rag man had a lot of original tunes? Yeah, and they used to play without a vowel key on it, you know? Mm-hmm. Play a real tune. That they made up themselves? No, they might have a ten-cent store.
No, I mean, the tune, did they make up themselves? Yeah, that's right. Well, the so-called street cries weren't really street cries. I can remember them from when I was a little girl. In the East.

Yeah, I want... Sometimes, some of the notes were a real true note, but it was enough to give you an idea if you wanted to copy and add to it, you know? And by Bolden, he stole that thing from the rag man.
When did you first see Bolden, do you remember?
When I bought my first good horn.
How old were you then? Fourteen. Your first slide trombone.
No, the vowel trombone.
Was that a vowel?

How old were you? Do you remember? Fourteen. Well, uh... You said. I was, uh... You see, I was ten, played a job at the old horn. I guess it picked me. I was about eleven years old. It was a year later, I bought the horn, you know? Where, where did you meet Bolden? I was, uh... I just bought my horn from the Whirline Music Store. Where there, my sister was living in New Orleans, and I stopped with her, you know. Is that the first time you went to New Orleans? That's my first time, yeah. And I was running over the horn, running over. Blowing the sound, you see. I liked it. I blew it. I was running over the horn, or they tried it in the music store, and Bolden happened to pass by, and he heard the trombone out, and he knocked on the door.
You just walked him down the street, you remember?

Yeah. Uh, Jackson and... and Roberson Street. Uh-huh. I was on Jackson, and he heard the horn, and he stopped, and he rapped on the door. I came to the serial man, he said, are you going to trombone? I said, yeah. Yes, sir. He said, well, you know who I am? I said, I don't really. He said, I'm the king. I said, king who? He said, Bolden. I said, no, hey, Mr. Bolden. He said, uh, you live here? I said, no, not exactly. My sister lives here. I live out in the country. He said, but I'd like to have you to work with me. I tell you sound very good. Is that so? He must have been. I said, I've been. I've been. I've been. I've been. I've been. I've been. I've been. I've been. I've been. I've been. Yes, that's so. He must have stayed out there and had me play. Because the first day you were trying out this new instrument. Yes. And, uh, so I said, wait a minute. I was so tickled, you know. I thought, oh, man, I'm going to play with King Bolden. I'm like my sister, I said, come here. I said, explain to my sister what you want. She said, oh, no, he had to go back home. He can't leave home that he's 21 years old.
Oh. What do you look like Bolden? What kind of a man was he? Can you describe him physically?

Yeah, he was kind of on a Moroni style look, you know. His hair went black and more exactly red. I see. Red and... And black. And they never combed it, it was always just way out of a cutty loose there. Was he big or small? Well, it's the time I saw him then, he was the size of, I say, Jim Robinson, but not quite as tall.
I see. Strong, strong man.
Strong man. Strong, yeah, strong man.
Was he dark skinned?
No, brown skinned. Brown skinned. And he never practiced in the house, he practiced on the box step out in the street, on the sidewalk.
Oh yeah?

He blows so loud he blew everyone out of the house when he practiced. Then he get out on the sidewalk and on the step and practice the tune and the kids are all gang around, King Baldwin, King Baldwin. Girls? Girls, boys and kids. Everything. Yeah. School kids and all.
How old was he when he came into the store there, do you think?
Who? Bolden.
How old was Bolden?
To his house. Oh, to his house. Oh, I never know Bolden, right age, you know.
But he was a grown man, actually.
Oh, yeah. Well, what? Do you think he was in his 40s?
Or in his 30s?
Well, yeah, he was about 37, 37 and 40.
What did his face look like?
Well, he had a round face. Plump or? Yeah, plump and not very tall. He was well big but not a tall man, you know. Anybody that you know that resembles him at all?
Did he have a spread nose, sort of like the one you describe as a meat nose? Meat nose, no.

Meat nose, no. Yeah, a fair, pretty nose. They were having good. Wouldn't brag off everybody. It was okay. It was a definite nose and not something special. So you didn't get to play with it? No, he wouldn't let me stay. I wanted to. But you had made a promise. I made a promise to my mother and dad. I would live with my sister until I was 21. And I did. I was 21, 4, 30 in the morning and 8 o'clock I was on the train. Made it for New Orleans, I've been gone ever since. Really? Yeah. I stuck to my promise.
Did you stay in Laplace until you were 21 years old?

Yeah, and I bought my sister a home. She didn't have a home, I bought her together. In Laplace? Yeah. Called Cherokee Town, it's a village, you know, something like this. Uh-huh, uh-huh. I bought a home for what good she did for me after I got all some money.
Uh-huh. She died in that home.
She died in that. Until you were 21, what did you do in Laplace?

Well, I worked in the sawmill a while, you know. So I bought the house, I bought the lot first in there. Uh-huh. And I bought green lumber, you know. Uh-huh. Just come out from the saw and he told me if I could get a wagon to haul it from my lot, and I was dried and that I could build. And Cypress, too. Yeah. And I wanted to take a mortgage on my lot. He had so much confidence in me, he wouldn't want any mortgage, he just trust me. And I built a house.
Well, did you keep up the music all the way through?

Sure, I played. We can. That's how I played between Baton Rouge, Laplace and Baton Rouge. All the plantations? All the sawmill towns. All the society halls, you know. Uh-huh. Every weekend I played. Did you keep pretty busy? Yeah, every weekend. Could you make pretty good money?
Yeah. What kind of places did you play in usually?
Dance halls. What did they look like? Picnics. Picnics. Looked like another country dance hall, you know.
Were they similar to the halls in New Orleans? Yeah. Like the economy hall and so on? Some, yeah.

Same idea? Some was just as large, some was as large as that and some was larger. Well, they were... They were owned by societies, you know. Out in the country? Yeah. Similar to our grange halls of the Dyson. They'd be packing jam, too.
So when you were 21 years old you came to New Orleans, huh?

To live, yeah. But I, after, I bought my first good horn, then I, I felt like I wanted to go to New Orleans, you know, the 90th century, you know, to go there. Yes. So I'd go on weekends, I mean, on Mondays, I'd work Sundays, sometime I'd go through, wouldn't stop in the process, go to catch the dance on Monday at a lawn party, you know. In New Orleans? Yeah, the other bands play.
Did you listen to a lot of the other bands?
Yeah, it was Clem, Bolin, and... Clem had a band, huh? Yeah. Was he a cleft player? Trumpet. He was kind of blind, like, you know.
Mm-hmm. Robichaux was the other one?
Three brothers. Johnny, Ed, and... What's the other bass player there? I've forgotten his name.
The old dad. What was your favorite band, then, when you were going into town, like, once in a while, like that? Uh...
Bolin was my favorite band. Bolin.
And Robichaux. What was your favorite?

It was Keppard. Oh, well, Keppard came up later. That's later. Keppard came up just by the time I did New Orleans. He used to play violin, you know. I met him out in the country with my little band. He came out there. Who was playing violin? He's Freddie Keppard.
Is that so? Yeah. Before he played the cornet, huh? Yeah. Mm-hmm.
And we were playing about three miles from them, and we sold out with no more beer, no liquor, no food to sell, and so we got off about an hour early, and we went down where he was playing.
Did he have his own little group?
Yeah. And he asked me to play with him. I played with him. How was his violin playing? We had all the karate.
Was he a fair violinist?
I had a guy who? Keppard. Oh, nothing to write home about. Uh-huh. But he was a good boy and a trumpet.
Was it a homemade violin or a regular violin?

No, a regular violin. Yeah, we was playing a real instrument then. And he was too? We were professional. We were playing professionally then. Yeah. That's how I met Freddie. Mm-hmm. And the guy playing baritone for trombone in the band. He had no trombone, he played a baritone. You know, plays with trombone. Willie Cornish.
Willie Cornish. Yeah.
You mean a brass baritone horn? Yeah. Yeah. I asked him, I said, why are you playing the baritone? He said, that's the best I could do. I'd have anything else to play on.
Well, at least he was honest about it. Yeah. Were the Holy Rollers a pretty big group?

I mean, did they do a lot of singing? Oh, yeah, they had drum and piano, a lot of singing, you know, clapping their hands. Spirituals though. Yeah. Well, Gospel. Gospel. Yeah, Gospel. Well, even the Baptist, some of the Baptist churches had it.
What, what was your religion? What? What was your religion at this time?
Catholic.
Were you born a Catholic? That's right. So you didn't go to Holy Roller churches or anything like that?
I don't want that to hear. Did you ever go to listen a little? Oh, sure, I dug it. I picked you up on a little.
Everyone else did too, if they were honest enough to admit it.
Sure.
Because that's where it really started.
They had some instruments there sometimes, huh? In church.

Well, yeah, there was a guy there, you know, just like we would call a, you know, a guest on a show or something. Yes. Well, I had guests, I'd invite trumpet players, trombone players to come over. And everybody would sing. Yeah, I would sing. You'd have to swing.
That's the way they sent the message, boy. Yeah. Must have been great, too. See, what we did. Thank you.
I heard that at Belmore, New Jersey.

60 years behind what happened, you know. I had to guess, you know, guest artists on the show. Same darn thing. Wasn't in the name for it. We invited things as one. We used to go over and listen. That's a nice, you know. That's been going on since I was a kid.
Well, was Make Me a Pallet on the floor?
That was a popular memory.
A spiritual before it was a...
Well, the first one I played was Bowlin, and he claimed it, so... Well, that was Bowlin's song. It was.
That's a profane song, if I ever heard of it. I thought maybe...
Yeah, I don't think it would fit in the church. I thought maybe that's... Not in the lyrics, no way.
No.
Unless they added a new lyric, you know.
After all, it was about an illicit love affair. I know, but I thought maybe, you know, Bowlin had added different lyrics to it or something like that.
Who knows, you know?
No, he did everything. But a lot of the numbers that they whipped up, they took old classical folk songs and all sorts of things and changed them over.

Last time I saw Bowlin, King Bowlin, I saw him at Masonic Hall. And he had a little trouble. I would stay there until the dance was over on a Monday night. And they shot... They'd spent all the deposit he'd receive on engagement. And when they paid him the rest, he'd had enough money to finish paying the boys, you know. So he started issuing it out. He said, yeah, it was your Colorado boys. He looked at that and he had 60 cents left. He said, this is for Chucky. No one gonna get this for Chucky. And he's Chucky. And he walked away.
Chucky?
Yeah. What does that mean? His wife.
That's the last time you saw him, huh? Yeah.
Next time he heard of him, he'd gone crazy. Yeah, he was in Jackson, Mississippi. Yeah.
Oh, he lived for years afterwards. He claimed the poison, I don't know. He put something on his mouthpiece.
Yeah. Oh, really? Is that what he said?
Some of the women... Oh, no. Oh, that's what the people said. Yeah, they run through the grapevine, you know. Yes. Oh, but he had lots of women.
Now, tell me. When you were 21 years old, exactly, you left Laplace and moved... Is that right? Moved to New Orleans. That's right. The very day.

The very day. I told him... Christmas day. He got on the train. I told him I was 21 and 8 o'clock I was on the train. And I had three miles to walk to get the train. And I walked in with bound time and I got on that train. I've been gone ever since.
And that was your final... Yeah. Your permanent leave of New Orleans.
Yeah. Of Laplace.
I mean, of Laplace. So when you arrived in New Orleans, that was in 1907, in other words, if you were 21 years old. Right? 1907. So what did you do when you arrived in New Orleans?

Well, I went to work in Stouroville with a guy named George John until I could get my band there. George Jones? George. George Jones. The boys' best players in the world. If the world could... You mean you were playing in the district?
Yeah. Where? At Pete Lallus. At Pete Lallus. With George Jones.
That was your first job in the city? Mm-hmm.
Yeah. What kind of a place with Pete Lallus? And my brother had a saloon right across from Stouroville in Conta in Claiborne. You know where that... Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.

I had a saloon there. Oh, your brother had a saloon? Yeah. And he had upstairs, and I had a nice room, you know, and having a rent to pay. He was married. He didn't live there. He just gave me a place to stay, and I... Was he older than you? Two years... Two years older. Two years older. Yeah, he was a businessman, you know. Mm-hmm. Over there, grocery and balls, his life. Well, he went in the rice field business. He made a little money, and invested.
What was Pete Lallus like? What kind of a place was it?
Oh, it was something like Tin Angel, but it was just a little cleaner, you know. A little cleaner. Mm-hmm. Oh, but...
Don't put that on there.
Don't worry about it. Do we forget that? Spit that for it. I'll make a few bucks.
Was it about the same size?
No, I think Tin Angel, a little larger. A little larger. Was it shaped the same way? Yeah, square. Square. And the bar was in the front, you know.
The bar was in front?
In front on... And where was the back? On Condite Street, and the building, you know, just right on the very corner.
Yes.

And where was the bandstand? Bandstand was... The back... The bandstand, when you sat down, your back was towards Canal Street. It was one block from Canal Street, you see? Mm-hmm. It was facing the bar, then. Mm-hmm.
So the bar was on this side, and the bandstand was on this side, across from each other? Yes.

No, the bar... The bandstand faced the bar, the bar was right on the corner, and the building went down that way. And the bandstand was here? Yeah, facing the bar. Facing the... With the back to Canal Street, when you sat down.
Was it a raised bandstand?
Yeah. Raised? Say, about this high. About that high from the floor?
Yeah. About five... Four or five feet.
That's right.
And how many pieces did you have there? Did... Huh? George Jones, how many pieces in his groove?
Well, he first had three, then he added me at four. Then... Then after...
You were playing valve trombone?
Yeah.
Valve trombone with him?
Yeah.
What were the other instruments?
Hmm. White bass and guitar. Yeah. The piano. What kind of people came to beat Lauderdale? Who?
What kind of people came there?
All kinds. The race house people. Oh, he had a good spot there.
Yeah. Did they have girls, B-girls and so on?
Look like sometimes I had C-girls.
Maybe all up there, I was.
Yeah. Love it. Did they have hustlers there? And was it... Sure. Was it a house like... Like... Was it a house like that? No, no. It was a meeting place.

I mean, the girls were there huffling on, you know, down the streets, you know, down the blockers crib, you see. Well, they make them a few dollars, they close up, you know, and say, well, I'm going to the cavalry and why they come in, you know, and then pick up some guys and go back, you see. Mixing business and pleasure. A lot of action, huh? Oh, man. Clockwork.
What time did you start working there? Eight to four. Eight to four. Eight to four, huh?
Long hours.
No union. How much money were you making? A dollar and a half a night and tips, but George didn't steal from us. So how long did you stay there?
Well, I stayed there about three weeks. Oh, that's all. And then?
Well, I got enough money and I sent for my band.
Oh, you sent for your own band?
Mm-hmm. Then I rented me a wagon and I had two signs made and advertised my band.
What did the sign say? Do you remember exactly?
Huh? New band in town.
New band in town.
Yeah, from Laplaccia, Louisiana. Kedora.
No, it wasn't Kedora.

No, it was Woodland Band. Woodland Band. Yeah. Woodland? Kedora's manager, yeah. Woodland? Woodland. Woodland Plantation. In one word? That's my dad's... Woodland. Woodland, yeah. W-d-a-l-a-n-d. Yeah. And I advertised it all over town. I rented a wagon. I had to sign made. What was it? I had my phone number, brother's telephone number, headquarter, Corn Iron Claybone.
Oh, you put the phone number
and the address? Everything. Boy, in the phone, started ringing.
It didn't say Kid Ori, dear. You had the name Kid then.
No.
No, no, she said that.
No, I should know. Woodland Band. Woodland Band.
But you said Kid Ori manager.

Ori, yeah. You weren't Kid Ori. You're right about that. I'm glad you're correcting. And so I advertised the band. I had my telephone, address and telephone. Headquarter, Corn Iron Claybone. Telephone.
Do you remember the telephone number?
Huh?
Remember what the phone number?
I know it was mean, but I don't know what was there. So when the phone started ringing, first job I got to the Globe Hall.
Oh, you mean you just paraded with nothing else in sight?

Anybody wants to say and call up? See, the first thing, the first time that ever happened in the morning that a band advertised themselves that way was no newspapers then, you know, no magazine advertised, you know. You didn't get that. You had to go for yourself. So I had an idea and said, well, let the people know I'm here. Nothing happened. I sent the boys home. I'm working in Storerville. Did you have a,
did you have a wagon with horses? Yeah. I mean, two horses? Two horses, yeah. And what, what was the wagon like? Oh, a furniture wagon, you know,
you saw the picture of it. How did the band sit in it? Oh, it's just there. I mean, like this? Yeah, it just sat with the face to the back of the wagon. Yeah, that's what, yeah.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah, tailgate on there. I was on there.
Did it have a thing on top?

Huh? No, I, I wasn't able to get one of those, you know. So it was open. This was the open. This was an open. That's what I wanted. But they called it drain. Two signs on each side was closed, you know, the music sat in the back, you see. Uh-huh.

If you'd been born here in America, Nessie, you'd have seen a lot of them when you were a kid. Mm-hmm. They were still around. Even in my hometown. Well, I'm too young. See, I was only born 18 years ago. I was, I was, I was, I was, I was, I was, you and Jack Paddy.

The wagon had high sides on it then, huh? Or just, No, they, the, the, the science, the science made the sides. Oh, so they come up about this, look, Oh, you put two big sides on each side. Then I had hand dodges, you know, throwaway cars. Was it the same side exactly on both sides? Yes, same, the same thing, yeah. We had the same words on both sides. Either side, I stopped, any corner, when I stopped play, to play, they could read, you see. People on their side could read, too. Who made the sign? Huh? Who made the sign? Oh, some guy around there made, I bought him a couple bottles of beer, he made them.
Was he a sign painter?
Yeah, he just liked me. I didn't charge me anything.
Didn't charge you anything?

He made them about five minutes. I say make them large and so people read them quick, you know. Who would have to spell? And the phone started ringing. First job I got was Globe Hall. Globe Hall? Yeah, it was the famous hall in there. Right in the old basement. Mm-hmm. St. Louis and Cleburne, and Cleburne and actually Robinson.
Mm-hmm.
And then I started working. Oh, it was a dance? Yeah. All right. Compassionate was about 2,000 people.
Oh, yeah?

They tore it down later. Then I started working over in Gretchen weekend. And finally I began playing with the economy all cooperatives all by and by. And I later I began working for the young yacht club, country club.
And all the society
parties too.
All the society
part of them down St. Charles Street. More money, you know. I got away from the chief skates.
Did you play much in the district? During lunch.

During lunch. You could get a job any time you want. Mm-hmm. All you're walking out your band look and see there's no band. Say, where you guys going here? You want to work here? I don't know. What you paying? A dollar and I'd go. You kept eating, you know. But you could buy so much for the dollar and a half. And you pick up probably dollar and a half tip sometimes.
You mean you only work in the district during Lent? Why is that?
Catholic time there. The Catholics didn't dance. During Lent? Yeah.
Oh, I see. Everything shut down.
I see.
He didn't want to just stand in the district like
Jilly Roll.
They're not dancing.
They're good Catholics. They start dancing Sunday night.
You know that Jilly Roll Morton never played outside the district?
Never. Did you know Tony Jackson?
Yeah. We didn't know Tony like me. Tony and Jilly would install Sturvey like piano plays, you know, single, you know. The two albums? Mm-hmm. People like Tony better if he sang, you know. He sang.
What kind of voice did he have?
Huh? What kind of voice? Nice, very nice. I wish I could
have a recording. Like a baritone or a tenor?
No, he was on most on the tenor like him.
High, high voice.
He had good octave, you know.
Yeah? It was pretty...
Yeah. He was on... Big on the queer side. Yeah. He was a young lady.
Oh, God. Where'd he play in the district?
Who?
Tony.

Oh, he played in different houses, you know, Lola White. All around. They did move around, you know. Jolly did too. Yeah, they did, you know, the fallout, you know, get people lay off and say, well, I'm going to rest and something like that.
Mm-hmm.
You know, I could get a job. Wasn't there any doors in the place. The place, the place was open 24 hours a day. No doors on the bar. Is that so? No. In the district, you mean? Mm-hmm.
All day and all night?
Yeah, they threw the doors away.
They threw the doors away. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm. So, once, how long did it take you to get established, you know, to get pretty well-known in New Orleans with your own band?

Well, I'd say about two months time I was gone. About two months you were, you had it, huh? and later then I found out the guys were making so much money off of me and I chartered two haul on late days. stuff

you know, before I left. You, you said? Economy Hall and Cooperative Hall. What? I, I tied them up for a whole year, you see. I rent both halls and I promote. Is that so? Yeah, I had Buddy Pitti working for them when I couldn't, I put him in the other hall and couldn't get in my place with the old guy.
So he's making money off both of them. So, so you. And some of them he rented, you didn't tell, and kept dark.
What?
You rented some more halls and kept them dark.
Yeah.
But he didn't win any competition at all.

Well, I did the, that's the one I'm speaking of cooperatives. I kept it dark until I couldn't accommodate people at the Economy Hall. Then later, well, I find out there's too many people and I opened it up. I had both of them opened.
How long did you keep the, the name Woodland Band?
Until I went and went to Lincoln Park. When was that? And the women all started calling me kid in Lincoln Park.
The following summer.
The following summer. Mm-hmm. And this guy Buddy Bottler, he was the promoter, you know.
At Lincoln Park? Mm-hmm. What kind of place was Lincoln Park?
Oh, big, nice place. Big, had a, a skating ring and a big pavilion. That was a roller skater. What kind of skating ring? Skate on skates. Roller skates.
Roller skates.
Yeah.
Mm-hmm. Double as a dance bar. And the pavilion?
Huh? And the pavilion? Pavilion, yeah. And the balloons used to go up every Sunday afternoon. And Buddy Bottler used to go up, you know.
Oh, yeah?
Until he came down with through a chimney like this, you know. Really? Yeah.
He made up his balloon a sense after that.
Who was that? Buddy Bottler. This guy put on this, uh...
He was a promoter at Lincoln Gardens.

Yeah. Buddy what? Bottler. Bottler. Buddy Bottler. How do you spell his name? B-O-T-T-L-E-Y, Bottler. Bottler. Buddy Bottler. Didn't somebody say Buddy Bowler went up and blows? No, no. That's Bottler.
His name's got confused. This is the guy, this is the guy. The promoter at the park where Bolden was playing at that time. I see. He's the guy, yeah.
And he came down at Kinnery? He's the one.
That's what after, that's why he gave up going up the balloons.

He's the one who invented this dance ping pong. I didn't know that, no. Yeah. Well, he's the one. Is that son? Yeah. Well, he used to work for the, the guy owned the place and when the guy, I don't know what happened if he died or what, then Buddy taking it over. Buddy was a big shot then, you see.
Buddy Bolden, you mean? Yeah. No, Buddy Bottley. Bottley. Uh-huh. Don't get the Buddies mixed up. Well, didn't, didn't Buddy Bolden work at Lincoln Gardens?

Uh, Lincoln Park? Yeah. Yeah. He worked at that too. Well, I finished telling you. Uh, he was speaking about me at Lincoln Park. So, it was a woodland band, you know. So, when Buddy hired me to play at Lincoln Park, I was there about two Sundays. On the third Sunday, then I walked up to the place, I saw the sign up there on, on the boulevard, you know. You know, they'd buy a kid over here, you see. I said, see, where you get the idea of the kid? You know what the girls call you? You're the kid from now on. You wouldn't give him the name. Buddy.

Oh, that's the way you got the name. I always wished on him. Uh-huh. And it stuck. Well, why did the girls call you kid? Hmm? Why did they call you kid? Well, it's more young, you know. Honey, be honest.
Tell him what the real meaning of it is. Well, I don't know. If they thought a guy was very nice looking. That's right. And very sweet, and they sort of went for him. They called him OU kid.
Love my wife with OU kid.
That's where that number came from later.
Yeah.
It could apply to either sex. And they kept calling him kid because, after all, he was young and sweet looking to them.

He still is. Still is. In a way. And so that's why I got the name kid. Now, if you understand about Bartlett, Bartlett Bowling. Yeah. Brother, Bartlett Bowling. Yeah, dark red. Robichoux used to play before I started playing there, you know. You can't play all the way back. And he.
Kid Ori, April 20th, 1957, reel three.

And he was very, very, very good looking. I've seen pictures of him. I'm so, what did you say? I used to see what his father looked like. He was so doggone good looking, it wasn't even funny. Yeah, I have a picture of that. He's in the bottom of the trunk out in the garage so it wouldn't get ruined.

And finished telling you, before I started playing there, you know. Yeah. When I used to go from Laplace, you know. Yes. Robichoux used to play every Sunday, afternoon, Sunday night. Uh huh. But the Bowling would play out, well, Malling Bird or Milling Bird, they called it then. Yeah. And that night Bowling would come, they'd have a skating ring in the afternoon in the, you know. Uh huh. One place would dance in the pavilion, the balloon would go up, but it probably used to go in the balloon. Well, that night, Buddy Bowling would come in and wake the skating ring and have the dance. Both places would run. You know, on the same ground.

Did you ever see Al Capone?

I knew Al. Hmm? Sure. You did know him? Yeah, all the boys, yeah. Yeah? Did you work with him? Gang, yeah. No, I didn't wake for him. He used to come in the club. Uh-huh. Plantation all the time. The plantation, huh? They used to bring him liquor. Good liquor. The guys, they were very nice to me. Probation time. They used to give me the best liquor to let me drink now.
Really?
Give him a fifth.
What did they do when they came to a club?
What? What did they do? They sat around and drink and have a good time. Put their guns on the table, Bob. Did they have girls with them? At times. At times.
Sometimes just...
No, just men.
Just men. What was the plantation club like?
It was one of the finest clubs in those days.
What part of Chicago was it?
I was on 35th and Calumet. You know, between South Park and Calumet. One block from South Park. The nest was right across the street. Sunset was over this way. Three clubs right there.
Do you mean the nest at the nest?
Yeah, after I was... Louis was across the street. At the Sunset? Yeah. Three clubs there, right there.
Three clubs right there. Was it a big club? Oh, yeah. Plantation? Yeah. Was it an after-hours place too? No. Oh, not a ginger.

Legit place. Yeah. That's a microphone. I know. It's good business. Very good. What did it look like? Every thing you say is recorded in that. What did it look like? A plantation? Yeah. Well, I tell you, there was... Well, I forget there. But 25 years ahead.
Oh, yeah? How's that?

I mean, and... Be in a nice-looking club, a nice-looking place. The atmosphere was fine. The acoustic was good. What band were you working on? Nice bandstand. Everything was up. Nice rug on the floor. Table there. People dance there? Yeah.
Did they have a floor show?
Floor show.
They did? What kind of shows did they have?
Huh?
Did they have a floor show?
Yeah.
What kind of shows did they have? What kind of entertainment?
All different kind of shows. That guy used to produce a show. They have different every four weeks. They changed, you know.
Did they have a line? Did they have chorus girls? Oh, yeah.
Dave Payton used to write music for them.
Oh, Dave Payton. Did he have the band, too? Who? Was it his band? Dave Payton's band? Oh, King Oliver's band. Oh, King Oliver's band.
He used to write some tough music there, too.
So you had to do a lot of reading in that band, huh?
That's for the show.
Who was hanging around with, who would come in with Capone?
Oh, I don't know the guy's name.
Oh, were many of them come in together, or just a few of them?
Oh, sometimes at times. Mostly there would be big gangs here, you know. stuff

Did you play the, was it a band similar to your own band?
Huh?
Was it the same kind of a band as yours?
Yeah. Then Freddie had, Freddie was very powerful, you know, trumpet player. He really played lots of trumpet down there.
Was he the best trumpet player in the city?
Sure. Until Joe came up, you know, with a different style, you see. Yeah. Well, Freddie, at that time, Freddie had gone, you know, had left. Yeah.
Did you use mutes much, Freddie, or did you play open most?
No, I never seen Freddie use mute yet.
Open, huh? Always open. Did you do much playing in the streets?
Who? Your band.
Yeah. Advertising and so on?
Advertising more than a band I've ever been in all names.
Really?

It pays to advertise. When did you advertise? Oh, it depends on time. I'd be busy on Sundays. I'd plan out at the lake. You know, picnics. You know, and have a dance Monday night. I'd have a dance in the week. In the week? Kennedy. Is that so? Yeah, I see where I could do it. You see? Just take it late in the afternoon, you know. Where did you play? Catch the people. Huh?

Oh, different pavilion out there.

Private homes, yeah. Tranchinas.
Did you play at Tranchinas? Mm-hmm. Did you play in Spanish 4th?
Yeah. Bucktown.
Bucktown?

Oh. Huh? That was my main house. What happened? Tell them. Well, we were fighting until we wanted to get tired of bands. Tired looked like I always went out.

Yeah.

Uh-huh.

Louie didn't know many numbers when he came with you either. No.
How long after that did Joe Oliver die? Oh, Joe Oliver died in 1937 or something. A long time. But all those years he lived in misery.

And he's broker than the Ten Commandments. I heard Louie pay for a funeral. I don't know. That's what I heard, yeah. Where'd he die, George? Yeah, I think he did. And taking his ballot to New York. You don't?
I don't think he popped as much as he does now.
I know he didn't. Because when I saw him, first in person was night.
Huh? I think he had a sister. A sister?
Yeah. I don't know. I'd love Joe the good old boy to play.
Could he play?

segments.title: Opening of the Kid Ory interview, San Anselmo
segments.summary: Allen announces the date and place; Mrs. Ory is heard in the background.

segments.title: Born in Laplace, Louisiana, on Christmas Day 1886
segments.summary: Ory gives his birth date and the exact distance from Laplace to New Orleans.

segments.title: Building homemade banjo, guitar and bass as a boy
segments.summary: At about seven Ory made a banjo from a bucket, strung with thread and fishing line, and a cigar-box guitar.

segments.title: No musicians in the family; the Laplace and Reserve brass bands
segments.summary: Nobody in his family played; he was drawn to the local brass bands.

segments.title: The homemade kid band, the Woodland Band
segments.summary: Ory, the Matthews boys and others formed a band of homemade banjo, guitar, soapbox bass and cigar-box violin.

segments.title: The humming band on the bridge
segments.summary: Before instruments the boys hummed harmony on a creek bridge at night, paid in ginger cakes.

segments.title: Rhythm instruments and the washtub drum
segments.summary: A wash tub deadened with rags and a foot pedal served as the first drum set.

segments.title: Promoting fish fries as a boy
segments.summary: Unable to get a job, Ory promoted fish fries and sold beer, catching the fish in the Mississippi.

segments.title: Prices and crowds at the fish fries in empty houses
segments.summary: He charged five cents a drink and held the dances in empty plantation houses at night for whole families.

segments.title: Tunes played and the Matthews brothers
segments.summary: The kid band played old tunes and waltzes; the Matthews boys were brothers, unrelated to Bill Matthews.

segments.title: Saving for a picnic and winning over his father's cousin
segments.summary: Ory saved fish-fry money to give a baseball-park picnic; the relative who doubted him changed his mind after seeing the crowd at a party.

segments.title: Buying real instruments and the band members
segments.summary: With picnic money he bought valve trombone, violin, twelve-string guitar, bass, trumpet and drum and named the players.

segments.title: Learning valve trombone by ear
segments.summary: Ory taught himself the valve trombone by trying brass-band horns and quickly played in all keys; the others were self-taught too.

segments.title: Following brass bands and ear training with the boys
segments.summary: As a child he hid under the bed to hear rehearsals, hummed harmony and bet on the keys bands played.

segments.title: Losing the family home and selling it for his sisters
segments.summary: The family place was mortgaged; Ory sold it and gave the money to his sisters.

segments.title: Promoting Saturday dances and the picnic admission
segments.summary: Dances were promoted by word of mouth on Saturday nights and Sunday afternoons, and the ballgame picnic charged 15 cents.

segments.title: Beer from his uncle's license and how the homemade instruments were made
segments.summary: His uncle supplied liquor; Ory describes burning f-holes into cigar boxes and breaking strings.

segments.title: New Orleans bands visiting Laplace on payday; Bolden's reputation
segments.summary: Ory had not been to New Orleans but heard Peyton, Galloway and others on paydays and knew Bolden's name.

segments.title: Bolden's excursion trains stopping at Laplace
segments.summary: Bands played from the baggage car at stops on the train to Baton Rouge as advertising for the dance.

segments.title: First job at ten and the cheap first valve trombone
segments.summary: Ory played up and down the road to Baton Rouge from age ten; his first horn cost $4 and had holes plastered with soap.

segments.title: Uniforms and clothes for the band
segments.summary: He bought matching coats from peddlers for the boys, with bow ties and cheap pongee suits.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: String bands and horn bands from New Orleans on paydays
segments.summary: Peyton's string band and Galloway's horn band played in big barns for dancing.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: Bolden's tunes came partly from Holy Roller church
segments.summary: Ory says Bolden took tunes like The Saints from the Holy Roller church and added his own feeling.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: Daughter Babette appears
segments.summary: Babette is brought in; Mrs. Ory tells how she blew kisses to a crowd at a train window.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: Bolden and the rag men's toy horns
segments.summary: Bolden also composed his own and borrowed ideas from rag men playing toy horns.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: First meeting Bolden at the New Orleans music store
segments.summary: While trying his new trombone, Ory was heard by Bolden, who invited him to join, but his sister refused.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: What Bolden looked like and how he practiced
segments.summary: Ory describes Bolden's hair, build and loud practising on the sidewalk step.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: Keeping a promise to stay in Laplace until twenty-one
segments.summary: Ory kept his promise to his parents, bought his sister a house and built his own, working in a sawmill.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: Playing country dance halls until 21
segments.summary: Every weekend he played society halls, sawmill towns and picnics between Laplace and Baton Rouge.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: Hearing New Orleans bands on trips; Bolden his favorite
segments.summary: Before moving he visited on Mondays to hear Clem, Bolden and Robichaux, and Bolden was his favorite.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: Freddie Keppard on violin and Willie Cornish on baritone
segments.summary: Ory met the young Keppard playing violin in the country and recalls Cornish playing baritone.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: Holy Roller churches, gospel singing and his Catholic upbringing
segments.summary: Church music of drums, piano and clapping is compared with guest artists on a show.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: Make Me a Pallet on the Floor as a spiritual or Bolden song
segments.summary: They debate whether the song began as a spiritual; Ory first heard it from Bolden.

segments.chapter: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
segments.title: Last time Ory saw Bolden
segments.summary: Ory recalls Bolden at Masonic Hall spending the money and rumors of his later madness.

segments.title: Leaving Laplace for New Orleans at 21
segments.summary: Ory left on his twenty-first birthday, Christmas 1907, and never lived in Laplace again.

segments.title: First job in Storyville with George Jones at Pete Lala's
segments.summary: He took a job at Pete Lala's with George Jones; his brother's saloon offered him a room.

segments.title: Layout of Pete Lala's
segments.summary: Ory describes the corner building, bar and raised bandstand.

segments.title: Band, crowd and pay at Pete Lala's
segments.summary: The band was four pieces, the crowd mixed, hours eight to four, pay $1.50 a night plus tips.

segments.title: Sending for his band and advertising from a wagon
segments.summary: After three weeks Ory sent for his Laplace band and advertised the Woodland Band by wagon with signs.

segments.title: The advertising wagon and sign
segments.summary: The band rode a furniture wagon with signs on both sides made by a friend.

segments.title: First jobs: Globe Hall, Economy Hall and society parties
segments.summary: The phone rang and he played Globe Hall, then the cooperative halls and society parties on St. Charles.

segments.title: Playing the district during Lent
segments.summary: During Lent Catholics didn't dance so bands worked the district.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton and Tony Jackson in the district
segments.summary: Ory discusses Morton staying in the district and Tony Jackson's singing and playing.

segments.title: The district with no doors
segments.summary: The district places were open day and night, with no doors on the bars.

segments.title: Becoming known in two months and renting both halls
segments.summary: Ory was well known within two months and rented Economy and Cooperative Halls to control the market.

segments.chapter: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
segments.title: Lincoln Park and promoter Buddy Bottley
segments.summary: Lincoln Park had a skating rink, pavilion and balloons; Bottley, the promoter, came down a chimney.

segments.chapter: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
segments.title: How Ory got the name Kid
segments.summary: Bottley put 'Kid Ory' on the sign after the girls called him Kid.

segments.chapter: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
segments.title: Bolden and Robichaux competing at Lincoln Park
segments.summary: Bolden's band played the skating rink while Robichaux played the pavilion, drawing the crowd with a horn out the window.

segments.chapter: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
segments.title: Jazz did not come from the African jungles
segments.summary: The Orys reject the idea that jazz came from Africa.

segments.chapter: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
segments.title: The pavilion versus the skating rink
segments.summary: The pavilion was bigger and the rink had the better floor.

segments.chapter: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
segments.title: The balloon and parachute at Lincoln Park
segments.summary: A canvas balloon, a parachute and a chimney landing.

segments.chapter: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
segments.title: Starting at Lincoln Park in 1908 after Robichaux
segments.summary: Ory followed Robichaux at the pavilion in summer 1908 and declined his offer.

segments.chapter: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
segments.title: Bolden's playing and what Ory thought of it
segments.summary: Bolden was rough and loud with no tone but deserves credit.

segments.chapter: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
segments.title: Replacing band members: Foster Lewis, Jake White and Eddie Garland
segments.summary: Ory lost a Laplace player and found bass player Garland through Manuel Perez.

segments.chapter: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
segments.title: How the girls dressed at Lulu White's
segments.summary: Ory describes the women in robes and house clothes.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong and leaving New Orleans
segments.title: First hearing Louis Armstrong and Joe Oliver on Labor Day parade
segments.summary: Ory heard a young trumpeter in the Labor Day parade and kept him in mind; Mutt Carey and Oliver played with Ory.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong and leaving New Orleans
segments.title: Louis sitting in with Ory's band at National Park
segments.summary: As a boy Louis sat in with the band and played Ole Miss and Keep Off Kelly's Head.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong and leaving New Orleans
segments.title: National Park and Louis wearing short pants
segments.summary: National Park at Third and Willow was a summer open ballpark dance.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong and leaving New Orleans
segments.title: Oliver and Noone leaving for Chicago
segments.summary: Ory's players Joe Oliver and Jimmie Noone took Chicago jobs, and he gave them $10 each.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong and leaving New Orleans
segments.title: The roughest place: Funky Butt Hall
segments.summary: Ory describes a dance hall that was also a church, where razors and guns were common.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong and leaving New Orleans
segments.title: Leaving New Orleans in 1919
segments.summary: He left for health and returned deposits, saying he was losing his health.

segments.title: Stopping in Los Angeles and sending for a band
segments.summary: On the way to Chicago he stopped in Los Angeles and sent for New Orleans players for a nightclub.

segments.title: Brass bands and funerals
segments.summary: He led a brass band when he wished and played funerals for gamblers and friends.

segments.title: The pimp's funeral with three bands
segments.summary: The biggest funeral he played was for a prominent pimp named Cook, with three bands.

segments.title: The first Ory records for the Spikes brothers in Los Angeles
segments.summary: The Spikes brothers asked him to record; the band traveled from Oakland to a shabby studio with megaphone horns.

segments.title: Making the first records in three hours and the tuxedo story
segments.summary: They recorded in one day in street clothes and deny the tuxedo story.

segments.title: Retakes and Dink Johnson on drums
segments.summary: Some sides came out first take; Dink Johnson stamped his feet so loudly a mattress was needed.

segments.title: Drummers: Ben Borders and Henry Martin
segments.summary: Ory rates his drummers and calls Henry Martin a metronome.

segments.title: Deciding to go to Chicago in 1925
segments.summary: He gave bands to former players who never did anything with them.

segments.title: Arriving in Chicago and first jobs
segments.summary: He sat in with Dixon, was hired by Cook and worked two jobs; he went to New York with Oliver in 1927.

segments.title: First Hot Five session and Dreamland with Louis
segments.summary: Louis wrote to Ory about recording together; Ory then worked Dreamland with him.

segments.title: Money from recording and lending at interest
segments.summary: Ory demanded double scale, lent money at 10% and left Chicago well off.

segments.title: Rehearsing in the studio
segments.summary: They rehearsed minutes at the studio, contrary to the claims of careful rehearsal.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton: Winin' Boy and his clothes
segments.summary: Ory describes Morton's walk, silk shirts, diamonds and pimping.

segments.title: Recording with Morton in Chicago
segments.summary: Morton wrote music for the records, which Ory says were not rehearsed much.

segments.title: Babette's jokes on Kid Ory
segments.summary: Mrs. Ory tells how Babette plays with the name Kid.

segments.title: What Ory wore in the 1920s
segments.summary: Ory describes eight suits, high roller hats and plain white shirts.

segments.title: Chicago clubs he worked in
segments.summary: Dreamland, Plantation, Sunset, White City and others, some with gangsters.

segments.title: Al Capone coming into the clubs
segments.summary: Capone visited the Plantation with guns on the table and gave Ory good liquor.

segments.title: The Plantation Club and its floor show
segments.summary: The Plantation at 35th and Calumet was a legit club with floor shows, Dave Peyton writing music.

segments.title: Rival gangs in the club and a shooting
segments.summary: Gangs sat on opposite sides; Ory once took cover behind a kitchen stove.

segments.title: Boyd Atkins's band and the St. Valentine's Day massacre
segments.summary: Ory was with Boyd Atkins and mistaken for a gunman on the morning of the Moran killings.

segments.title: Freddie Keppard's band
segments.summary: Ory liked Keppard's band best; Keppard was powerful, never used mute and had gone before Oliver rose.

segments.title: Advertising and playing around the lake
segments.summary: He advertised more than other bands, played lake pavilions, camps and private homes.

segments.title: Wagon band battles and playing soft
segments.summary: Ory rode an automobile truck to catch other bands and played softly to draw crowds.

segments.title: Tying wagons together and winning Joe Oliver
segments.summary: Black Benny tied wagons; Oliver was beaten and joined Ory, who corrected his tone.

segments.title: Last meeting with Oliver in 1928
segments.summary: Oliver, stranded in Georgia, thanked Ory for the king title.

segments.title: Oliver's decline and death
segments.summary: They discuss Oliver's poverty and death, and Louis not knowing many numbers.
